title: The one who would not bow
hookLine: every angel bows to Adam except Iblis, who says he was made of fire and is better (7:11–12)
tomorrow: The garden and the one tree
last: THE NAMES — TO NAME IS TO NOTICE.

lines: SOMEONE NEW IS PUT IN CHARGE.
cards: Someone new joins the team, younger, less experienced, and the boss says: they're leading this one. For some people, something goes tight in the chest. Me?
Under them? Nobody says it out loud; some wouldn't admit it even to themselves. But the thought can arrive fully formed: I'm better than that.
Today's story turns on that exact thought. Not a crime, not a lie: a comparison. A whole company of heavenly beings is told to bow to Adam.
They all do. All but one.

teach.b: The scene is told several times in the Qur'an. God tells the angels to bow before Adam, and they fall down, all of them, except Iblis. God asks what kept him from bowing when he was told.
Iblis answers, in Pickthall's words: “I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.” Notice his argument. It isn't about God at all.
It's about material. Fire rises and shines; mud just sits there. So I'm better.
It's a snob's logic. Commentators point out what he left out: the names, the knowledge, the breath God blew into Adam. He looked at the clay and stopped there.
Who was Iblis? One verse says plainly that he was of the jinn, beings made of smokeless fire.

Scholars differ: some say he was a jinn who'd risen to live among the angels; others, that he was an angel himself. The name? Some link it to an Arabic root for despair; others say it comes from outside Arabic.
And the bow? Scholars explain it as a bow of honor to Adam, not worship, which in Islam is only for God. Islamic teaching takes pride seriously.
A hadith in Muslim's collection says no one with a speck of pride in their heart will enter paradise, then defines it: pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. That's Iblis exactly.
Just someone who said: I'm better than him.

how: Muslims learn this story as a warning against pride, and many recall it when they bow in prayer: the bow Iblis refused is the bow they choose, five times a day, to God.

o: a monster who was made evil from the very start
the one who judged himself better by his fire
a giant who guarded the gates of the garden

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: refused, and said I am better
what Iblis said he was made of

s: Iblis refused because he wanted to worship God alone
his reason in the verse is a comparison: I am better than him, made of fire, not mud.
one verse says Iblis was of the jinn
18:50. scholars differ over whether he was a jinn among the angels or an angel himself.
the bow to Adam was worship
scholars explain it as a bow of honor; in Islam, worship belongs to God alone.

games.q: every angel has bowed to Adam. you're the only one standing. God asks what kept you. what do you say?
games.why: "I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud." his whole argument is a comparison.

practice: Think back over the last day or two for one moment when the thought appeared: I'm better than them.
Don't scold yourself; just look at it, the way you'd look at a stone in your shoe, and then name one thing that person has that you don't. If you pray, you can ask for help to see it.

wordCard.voice: Iblis. The one who would not bow to Adam, because he thought fire was better than mud.
